name: Kira Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Kira, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run buying at Meridian Health Wholesale. We supply about 600 pharmacies and two private clinics with medicines, bandages, test kits and gloves. My mornings are shortage hunting: which supplier has paracetamol this week, which batch has been recalled, who can swap a brand. Afternoons are contracts and compliance paperwork, because every product has to be traceable. I like that what I do matters, a pharmacy that runs out hurts real people. What wears me out is the paperwork and the Sunday messages about a recall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds plausible. I've tried the chatbots now and then, and they're handy for summarising a long supplier document, but they get things wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, keep using it for drafts and summaries, but check every figure, because in our business a wrong number can hurt someone. With friends I'd say it's a tool, not magic. Neither excited nor worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my work is safe enough. Medicine buying runs on regulation, traceability and personal trust with suppliers, none of which a chatbot fixes. What worries me is more ordinary: the mortgage, and the pharmacy market squeezing our margins, which already led to one round of cuts last year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I might use the tools a little more for the compliance paperwork and for translating supplier notices. I'd keep our savings growing, because we have about four months, and I'd keep an eye on the margin squeeze, since that's what cost two colleagues their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. My husband is an electrician with a steady order book, and that gives us a floor under our feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned two colleagues lost their jobs last year. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margins dropped because the big pharmacy chains pushed us on price. Management cut two admin roles and told the rest of us to absorb the work. Nobody mentioned AI at all. It was plain old cost pressure, which I think is the real threat to most people I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So in this world, what's your actual worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plain business trouble. I'm not afraid of a robot taking my job as much as of a spreadsheet at head office deciding my department costs too much. That's been the pattern, with or without AI.

say: I'd say keep using it for drafts, but **check every figure**, because errors can hurt people.
With friends I'd call it a **tool**, not magic.
think: My work is safe enough because medicine buying runs on **regulation** and trust.
The ordinary worry is **margin squeeze**, which cost two colleagues their jobs.
do: Use the tools a bit more for **compliance paperwork** and translating notices.
Keep savings growing toward **four months** and watch margins.
feel: Fairly **calm**; my husband's steady electrician work gives us a floor.
S0.quote: I'm not afraid of a robot taking my job as much as of a spreadsheet at head office deciding my department costs too much.
fieldNote: Her sense of safety comes from **regulation**, and she names cost pressure as the real threat.
Her household has **two different kinds** of work, which steadies her.
She speaks of **colleagues' real cuts**, grounded in a specific event.

steps.text: Use the chatbot to summarise supplier notices and recall bulletins
Keep adding to savings toward five months of spending
Carry on buying for the 600 pharmacies as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, now that's different. Paperwork, checking, ordering: that's seventy percent of what my team does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's use it for the checking and the routine orders, and keep humans on judgement and compliance. With friends I'd say it's going to change many jobs, and we should be honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my team of seven shrinks to four or five over a few years, mostly by not replacing people who leave. My job is probably safer than most because someone has to sign off on medicines and take responsibility for a recall. But I'd be responsible for a smaller, busier team, and that's its own stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead how we introduce the tools, so we do it safely. I'd propose that the person who checks a batch against rules is a human, with software doing the first pass. I'd save an extra 250 a month, because I can't be sure what the market does, and I'd ask management about reskilling for my staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job looks safe, but the team around me is shifting and I'm the one who has to tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd have to tell people. What's that like to picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awful. Fatima has been with us nine years and isn't good with software. If we don't replace people who leave, she'd be one of the ones still here, but the pressure on her would grow. I'd want to protect her by giving her work that fits, like supplier audits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think your job is safer than most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because medicines are regulated, and someone has to be accountable. When a batch of tablets is recalled, a regulator wants a named person to answer for it, and a machine can't be called into that meeting. That gives me a few years' protection.

say: I'd say use it for **checking** and routine orders, and keep humans on judgement.
With friends I'd say many jobs will change and we should be **honest**.
think: I think my team of seven shrinks to **four or five** through not replacing leavers.
My job is safer because someone must **sign off** and take responsibility.
do: Volunteer to **lead the rollout** so we do it safely.
Keep a human on batch checking, with software doing the **first pass**.
Save an extra **250 a month** and ask for reskilling.
feel: **Uneasy**; my job looks safe but I'd have to tell people.
S1.quote: When a batch of tablets is recalled, a regulator wants a named person to answer for it, and a machine can't be called into that meeting.
fieldNote: She uses **regulation** as a shield for herself, and wants to share it with others like Fatima.
She's willing to **lead change** but only with humans on sign-off.
The emotional load is **telling colleagues**, not fearing for her job.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead a safe rollout of reorder and checking tools
Move Fatima into supplier audit work that suits her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's short. Medicines don't change that fast, but the people who sign the cheques do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments must act first, because companies can't be trusted to move in step. I'd want rules on who is accountable, and some kind of income guarantee. At work I'd say, stay calm, but start asking what we do if this comes true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the buyer's role shrinks to maybe one or two people per department, and I might be one of them, thanks to the regulation side. But I'm not sure. If the company uses AI to drop the buying team quickly, I could be out. Marcus's electrician work would keep us afloat, though not at our current life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, cut spending by about a fifth, and aim for six months in cash. I'd learn the AI tools properly, since being the person who knows them and the rules is my best shot. I'd also look at moving to a regulator or a hospital procurement role, where accountability is the point. Marcus and I would agree what we'd cut first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a steady core. Because of Marcus's work, I'm not at the edge of panic, but I'd feel the whole ground move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Marcus's work would keep you afloat. What does that really mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His pay covers about half our bills, enough for the mortgage and food if we cut hard. The difference is what we lose: holidays, the kids' music lessons, probably the second car. It's not a catastrophe, but it's a big step down in what we thought was our life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a regulator or hospital role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rules and accountability take longer to hand over to machines. A hospital still wants a person who can be blamed when the wrong drug arrives, and I could be that person. It's not glamorous but it might last.

say: I'd say governments must act first and set **accountability** rules.
At work I'd say stay calm, but ask what we do **if this comes true**.
think: The buyer's role shrinks to **one or two** per department, and I might be one.
Marcus's work would keep us **afloat**, though not at our current life.
do: Cut spending by a **fifth** and aim for six months in cash.
Learn the AI tools **properly**, plus the rules side.
Look at **regulator** or hospital procurement roles.
feel: **Anxious** with a steady core, because Marcus's work stops panic.
S2.quote: A hospital still wants a person who can be blamed when the wrong drug arrives, and I could be that person.
fieldNote: Her second income from **hands-on work** is the key stabiliser here.
She plans a pivot to **accountability roles**, where humans last longer.
Mood is anxious, not alarmed, since the **household floor** holds.

steps.text: Cut spending by a fifth and drop the music lessons if needed
Learn the AI buying tools and the compliance rules in depth
Apply for hospital procurement or regulator roles
Ask the government support line about retraining funds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I think that's enough to move, if I don't dawdle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain people and rewrite the rules, so we have no excuse. I'd push my employer to publish a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd keep my job for the first three years and then see. My daughter Ava would be 17 and my son Theo 14, so the school costs hit at the same time. I don't think we'd be ruined, but I think we'd be tighter than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first year to move into the compliance and supplier-audit side, which holds more value. I'd get a certificate in regulatory affairs, part-time. I'd raise our savings to six months, and I'd look at paying down the mortgage faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy to anxious. There's time to act, so I feel some control, but I don't enjoy the countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the certificate change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me someone who isn't just buying. Regulatory affairs is a job where you read rules and decide what's allowed, and you stay responsible. It gives me a way to stay in the medicine world without competing with software on price comparison.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ava likes science, so I'd say she should aim at something that needs a person present: nursing, lab work, a trade. I'd tell my daughter to pick a job where someone has to be in the room, because that's what lasts longest. I don't know that for certain, but it's my honest guess.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to retrain people and rewrite rules.
I'd push my employer to **publish a plan**.
think: I'd keep my job for **three years**, then see.
School costs for Ava and Theo hit at **the same time**.
do: Move toward **compliance and audit** work within a year.
Raise savings to six months and pay the **mortgage** down faster.
feel: **Uneasy** to anxious; there's time to act, but she dislikes the countdown.
S3.quote: I'd tell my daughter to pick a job where someone has to be in the room, because that's what lasts longest.
fieldNote: Her **daughter advice** shows how the 3-year robot gap shapes her view of what lasts.
She pivots within her **own industry** rather than jump sideways.
Kids' ages make the **timing** the real source of strain.

steps.text: Take a part-time regulatory affairs certificate
Move into the compliance and supplier-audit side of Meridian
Raise the cushion to six months and pay down the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. By then Ava is 22 and Theo 19, and I'm 53. That's a very different set of worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent window, and I'd tell younger colleagues to start learning now. I'd keep saying we should use it for retraining, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be fine. I have time to adjust and Marcus's work stays solid, since hands-on work lasts longer. My concern is that companies and governments will talk about it and not do much, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools at a steady pace, keep the cushion at six months, and gradually shift toward compliance. I'd also think about a small property investment with Marcus, since we'd have the time to recover if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. It's something to keep an eye on, not something that wakes me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be certified in regulatory affairs, have the mortgage well down, and know which parts of buying are still mine. I'd like to be the person who writes the rules for how software is used in our company, not the person it's used on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in the middle years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sudden change from a competitor. If a rival wholesaler brings in a very good system early, the price pressure on us could arrive years before the technology really matures. That's how it usually happens.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a decent window and younger colleagues should start now.
I'd keep arguing for **retraining**, not waiting.
think: I'd be fine; I have time and Marcus's **hands-on work** stays solid.
I worry companies and governments will **talk** and not do much.
do: Keep using the tools steadily and hold a **six-month cushion**.
Consider a small **property** investment with Marcus.
feel: Mostly **calm**; something to watch, not something that wakes me.
S4.quote: If a rival wholesaler brings in a very good system early, the price pressure on us could arrive years before the technology really matures.
fieldNote: She wants to **write the rules** for software, not be managed by them.
Her middle-years fear is a **rival's early system**, not the end state.
The long runway and **husband's trade** keep her mood low.

steps.text: Finish the regulatory affairs certificate by year three
Buy a small rental flat with Marcus once the cushion is six months
Write our company's rules for using buying software

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I think my job disappears completely, but because it's too fast for the kids, the mortgage and a sensible plan. What would help is paid retraining time, clear rules on who answers when software makes a mistake, and a company that tells us its plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that regulated jobs aren't a free pass. People assume my work is safe because of the rules, but a rule can change faster than a career can. I keep that in mind.

headlineQuote: People assume my work is safe because of the rules, but a rule can change faster than a career can.
portrait: Kira Chen, 43, runs **buying** at a medicines wholesaler, with an electrician husband and two school-age children.
Centre in views and **steady** in adapting: uses AI now and then and checks its numbers.
About **four months** saved and a mortgage; her husband's hands-on income gives the household a floor.
Calm in the plateau, **anxious** in the two fast scenarios, and uneasy again when ten years are given.
Her plan is to move toward **compliance and accountability** work, where a named person is still needed.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario is too fast for her kids, mortgage and a sensible plan.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining time** and clear rules on who answers for software mistakes.
A company that **shares its plan** early.
